description:
We are "Rapadura Côsmica," a team of Computer Engineering, Computer Science, and Software Analysis students from Campina Grande, Brazil! Like our regional candy "rapadura"—tough, sweet, and full of energy—we build resilient solutions.

For NASA's Astronaut Health challenge, we are combining Java, Python, Front-end, and hardware prototyping to create a real-time health monitoring system for space missions!
summary: Rapadura Cósmica is an autonomous astronaut health monitoring and clinical decision-support platform built for deep-space missions where communication latency with Earth prevents real-time medical intervention. Using official NASA and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) spaceflight health research, our system continuously ingests and cross-correlates four critical biomarkers: Heart Rate (bpm), Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂ %), Orbital Radiation Exposure (mSv), and Sleep Duration (h). Unlike conventional dashboards that merely display isolated numbers, our clinical rules engine detects multi-signal anomalies—such as tachycardia combined with dropping oxygen saturation—escalating the mission status to CRITICAL, explaining the root clinical trigger, and displaying an immediate prioritized countermeasure aboard the spacecraft. Synchronized in aerospace standard UTC, the platform protects crews in orbit while offering direct transferability to remote telemedicine and extreme-environment monitoring on Earth.
details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS Rapadura Cósmica is an end-to-end, offline-capable telemetry and clinical triage ecosystem designed to empower spacecraft crews to recognize medical risks and act autonomously when Earth mission control is minutes away due to deep-space latency.

The platform operates through a modular multi-service architecture:

1. Telemetry Edge Simulator (telemetry-analytics/simulator): Generates realistic physiological and environmental telemetry streams across Nominal, Critical, and Dynamic flight scenarios in ISO 8601 UTC format.

2. Core Orchestration & Persistence Gateway (astronaut-health-api — Java 21 / Spring Boot): Receives incoming astronaut readings via REST endpoints, forwards payloads to the analytics engine, persists historical mission records in an embedded relational database (H2/JPA) with fault-tolerant fallback handling, and exposes the latest consolidated state.

3. Cross-Correlated Clinical Rules Engine (telemetry-analytics — Python 3.12 / Flask): Evaluates individual thresholds alongside multi-parameter clinical rules derived from NASA and CSA research (such as correlating elevated heart rate with acute hypoxia or radiation spikes with sleep deprivation) to classify risk (NOMINAL, WARNING, CRITICAL) and prioritize the single most urgent recommendedAction.

4. Mission Control Dashboard (mission-control-ui — HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JS): A high-contrast aerospace dark-mode interface refreshing every 3 seconds, displaying live vital signs, active clinical alerts, prioritized countermeasures, and UTC mission synchronization.

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT - In Space: Eliminates cognitive overload during high-stress orbital emergencies by turning raw telemetry into clear, actionable clinical guidance without waiting for ground support. - On Earth: The lightweight, containerized, zero-cloud-dependency architecture translates directly to remote telemedicine, maritime and offshore platforms, mining operations, and rural emergency triage where connectivity is intermittent.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES & ENGINEERING PRACTICES - Languages & Frameworks: Java 21 (Spring Boot), Python 3.12 (Flask), HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+). - Infrastructure & Testing: Docker, Docker Compose, Makefile automation, Git submodules, Pytest, and JUnit 5. - Hardware Concept: Conceptual wearable sensor prototype modeled on Arduino/Tinkercad. FUTURE ROADMAP - Expanding the clinical matrix to include Body Temperature (°C), blood pressure, and cabin CO₂ levels. - Integrating a local, low-context Small Language Model (Edge AI / SLM) onboard to provide adaptive natural-language clinical assistance offline. - Collaborating with aerospace medicine specialists for clinical threshold calibration.
